summary: An implementor's guide for the Internet Printing Protocol version 1.1, one of a set of documents describing IPP.

plainLanguage.summary: This guide offers practical advice for building IPP clients and printer objects. The IPP Model and Semantics and Encoding and Transport specifications take precedence if they conflict with this guide.

questions: what is the internet printing protocol
what is the ipp implementors guide
subtitle: Implementation advice for clients and printers using IPP/1.1.

tldr.problem: Implementers found unresolved details and differing interpretations while building and testing IPP implementations.
tldr.mechanism: The guide suggests request-processing checks, explains job validation and lifecycle behavior, and clarifies character sets, HTTP transport, and implementation issues.
tldr.outcome: It supplements the IPP model and transport specifications but is not part of the formal specification. It is Informational and obsoletes RFC 2639.

today: RFC 3196 is an Informational guide published in November 2001 that obsoletes RFC 2639. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: How the Guide Fits with IPP
sections.content:
The Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) is an application-level protocol for distributed printing. RFC 3196 supplements the IPP/1.1 Model and Semantics and Encoding and Transport documents and also discusses IPP/1.0 implementations.

The guide is not part of the formal IPP specification. If it conflicts with RFC 2911 or RFC 2910, those documents take precedence. The guide includes issues raised at three interoperability testing events.
sections.plainLanguage: This is supporting advice for people implementing IPP. The main IPP specifications take precedence if the documents disagree.

sections.title: Suggested Request Checks
sections.content:
The guide proposes checks an IPP object can perform when it receives a request. It may be strict and perform all checks, or more forgiving toward nonconforming clients; status codes can therefore differ between implementations. Clients should send conforming requests and should use Validate-Job before sending a large document.

The suggested checks include validating the version and operation, then checking required attribute groups, their order, and the values of required attributes. A printer may ignore an unknown attribute group in the expected position just before document content, because it may come from a later minor version.
sections.plainLanguage: A printer can check a request's version, operation, required fields, and values before accepting it. Clients should follow the specified format because forgiving printers may handle mistakes differently.

sections.title: Job Attributes and Job States
sections.content:
To validate a requested job-template value, compare it with the printer's supported value or range. Check each value separately when an attribute has multiple values. Unsupported attributes or values are reported in the Unsupported Attributes group; the result depends on the request's attribute-fidelity setting.

After a job is created, the printer schedules it and changes its state as it processes the job. A job may become completed, canceled, or aborted. Once the job object is removed, a request for it can return a not-found or gone status; the guide advises against reusing job identifiers too soon.
sections.plainLanguage: The printer checks each requested setting against what it supports and reports unsupported choices. A job's state changes as the printer schedules, processes, and finishes or stops it.

sections.title: Character Sets and Printing Details
sections.content:
IPP clients and objects are required to support UTF-8. The guide recommends that an IPP object also support US-ASCII and list the supported character sets. If an object supports both, it must accept requests in either and convert between them with the highest fidelity possible.

The guide also discusses printers that pause or stall, jobs sent to devices without status reporting, and printer URIs. A busy printer may use TCP flow control while processing a Print-Job rather than returning an error.
sections.plainLanguage: IPP implementations must understand UTF-8, and the guide recommends support for US-ASCII too. When a printer is busy, it may slow the data transfer rather than reject the job.

sections.title: HTTP Transport and Long Waits
sections.content:
IPP runs over HTTP. Clients and servers must support HTTP/1.1; HTTP/1.0 is an optional compatibility mode. Printers can wait for the full request before responding, so a client may need to tolerate a long delay while sending a document.

The guide says clients should avoid socket timeouts while sending jobs. A client may open another connection to ask for printer attributes while the original job is waiting. Chunked requests are required of IPP printers, and Transfer-Encoding must be present when Content-Length is absent.
sections.plainLanguage: A printer may take a long time to receive a job, so the client should not end the connection just because it is waiting. The client can use another connection to ask why the printer is delayed.

sections.title: Jobs Submitted Through Other Protocols
sections.content:
The guide refers readers to the security considerations in the IPP/1.1 Model and Semantics document. It adds advice for printers that also accept jobs through other protocols: those jobs should be queryable with Get-Jobs, even if some IPP job attributes are unknown.

Foreign jobs may belong to another user or to anonymous. The guide says only an authenticated operator or administrator may query them unless local security policy permits users to see other users' jobs; it assumes authentication and authorization have already occurred at a lower layer.
sections.plainLanguage: Printers that accept jobs through other protocols need rules for who can view those jobs. The guide assumes that authentication and authorization happen before the IPP request is processed.
